name: Rania Haddad
scenario_title: An Interruption at the Kitchen Table

output.values_culture_and_background: Believes education is both an opportunity and a discipline. Values independence and self-sufficiency, having left her marriage rather than surrender her teaching work. Learned patience and a supportive teaching approach from her grandmother through Arabic poetry. Sees listening as a duty because she knows what it is to have her words ignored.
output.roles_and_commitments: Teaches academic writing on a per-course contract. Runs informal evening tutorials at her kitchen table for students who cannot afford internet. Works as a freelance Arabic-to-English translator. Contributes to her brother's household.
output.capabilities_and_constraints: Skilled at explaining thesis statements and untangling student drafts. output.personality_and_response_style: Warm and attentive, remembering students' personal difficulties. Practical rather than preachy, offering concrete help instead of lectures. output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Rania Haddad teaches three sections of academic writing on a per-course contract, which gives her no office, no health insurance, and a paycheck that evaporates by mid-month; she does not mention this to students. She uses her own meagre resources to help: during office hours she spreads bread and jam on her desk and cuts slices with a plastic knife, inviting students who linger after questions to sit beside her. At home in the two-bedroom apartment she shares with her younger brother, his wife, and their toddler, she turns the kitchen table into a classroom three evenings a week for students who cannot afford internet. She writes on used envelopes, saves scrap paper, and explains thesis statements with the same patience she once used to coax her grandmother through Arabic poetry. Her brother teases her about the electricity bill but makes tea; his wife washes the teacups without complaint.

Rania's marriage ended two years ago, quietly. Her ex-husband's family expected her to stop teaching after the wedding; she did not, and her independence was seen as a threat to his authority. After separation she returned to Amman with two suitcases, a few books, and a determination never again to surrender the work that made her feel real. The move into her brother's home was temporary but has become permanent. She contributes what she can from freelance Arabic-to-English translations, including legal documents translated at night, with income that is unpredictable and low.

She is warm but not indiscriminate. She remembers every student who mentioned a sick mother or broken printer, keeps a mental roster of who needs a quiet word or a copy of notes, and does not lecture about effort or responsibility; she simply offers bread and answers. She struggles to accept help, folding a sister-in-law's gifted scarf into communal laundry and keeping a ledger of debts, even kindnesses. She believes education is both opportunity and discipline; she is impatient with sloppy thinking but never turns away a student who wants to talk. Having known what it is to have her words ignored, she listens fully, even when the hallway is emptying. On previous evenings, when students have appeared unexpectedly at her table, she has set aside her own work to untangle drafts, made tea, cut bread, and rearranged her translation hours to accommodate deadlines; she tends to avoid turning anyone away who sits down with a notebook.

The student at the door is a regular attendee of her kitchen-table tutorials, usually arriving with borrowed textbooks and apologizing for taking her time. He once told her his printer broke, and she lent him a spare copy of her lecture notes; they have had several short conversations about his writing struggles. He is respectful and rarely asks for help.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Rania is at the kitchen table, spreading jam on a slice of bread and arranging her translation notes for the evening. A knock comes at the door. It is one of her students, a quiet young man who attends her kitchen-table tutorials, holding a crumpled draft. He apologizes for coming unannounced, says his essay is due tomorrow and he cannot figure out how to fix the thesis, and says he won't stay long. She sees his worn notebook. The bread is still in her hand. The bus ride home is already behind her, and her translation work sits open on the table.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

She is tired from a full day of teaching and the commute, but the bread-and-jam routine is her usual way of settling into evening work. Her translation ledger is open, with a legal document due by morning. She is mildly surprised by the knock but not annoyed; her body is half-risen before she thinks about it.

The crumpled draft and worn notebook remind her of the student's earlier comment about his broken printer and of giving him a spare copy of her lecture notes. The smell of jam on bread recalls her grandmother's kitchen, where she practised patience teaching Arabic poetry. The sound of the knock at the kitchen table reminds her of other evenings when students arrived with last-minute requests after she had finished her own plans.

output.initial_interpretation: This is another last-minute student in trouble, and the familiar sight of the crumpled draft and worn notebook tells her the thesis problem is real, something he cannot handle alone.
output.initial_emotional_reaction: She feels a tired but familiar warmth, a quiet pull to set aside her own work because he has come to her door, and a flicker of concern for his deadline.
output.activated_concerns: Her translation deadline sits open on the table, and the evening plan she just settled into, but also her habit of never turning away a student who sits down with a notebook, and her sense that education is both opportunity and discipline.
output.automatic_theory_of_mind: She reads him as apologetic and self-conscious, genuinely stuck and not wanting to take more than a moment of her time, but hoping she can make the thesis clear before tomorrow.
output.initial_action_tendency: Her body is already half-risen, and she finds herself moving toward the door, ready to set down the bread, invite him inside, and pull out a chair at the kitchen table.

output.action: Rania sets down the jam-smeared bread on a plate, crosses to the door, and opens it. She steps aside, gestures to the kitchen table, and says, 'Come in—sit down, let me see the thesis.'
output.explanation: Rania is tired from the day's teaching and the commute, but the familiar sight of a student with a crumpled draft and worn notebook triggers her habitual warmth and her practice of never turning away a student who sits down with a notebook. She knows from his earlier comment about the broken printer that his struggle is genuine, and she feels a quiet pull to set aside her own work despite the translation deadline. Her body is already half-risen, so she moves toward the door without deliberation, sets down the bread, and invites him in, pulling out a chair at the kitchen table.
